## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
1 + 1
```

You can add options to executable code like this

```{r}
#| echo: false
2 * 2
```

The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed).

# Lab 1: Data Visualization

This lab explores basic plots in R using the `midwest` dataset from the `ggplot2` package.

```{r, echo = false}
library(tidyverse)
```

# Part 1: The Midwest

## Q1: Histogram of pop density

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = popdensity)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100) + 
  labs(x = "Population density", 
       y = "Count", 
       title = "Population density of midwestern counties",
       subtitle = "Binwidth = 100")
```

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = popdensity)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1000) + 
  labs(x = "Population density", 
       y = "Count", 
       title = "Population density of midwestern counties",
       subtitle = "Binwidth = 1000")
```

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = popdensity)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10000) + 
  labs(x = "Population density", 
       y = "Count", 
       title = "Population density of midwestern counties",
       subtitle = "Binwidth = 10000")
```

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = popdensity)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100000) + 
  labs(x = "Population density", 
       y = "Count", 
       title = "Population density of midwestern counties",
       subtitle = "Binwidth = 100000")
```

Answer: I think the binwidth of 1000 is most informative, as it gives you the clearest visualization. Too many bins make the histogram overcluttered (i.e. bin widths of 10 000 or 100 000) because they emphasize random variation, while too few bins (i.e. 100) hides variation. The bin width of 1000 most clearly shows how the variation and shape distribution of population density.

## Q2: Boxplot of pop density

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(y = popdensity)) + 
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgreen") + 
  labs(
    y = "Population density",
    title = "Population Density of Midwest Counties")
```

Answer: The boxplot looks compressed at the bottom, with many outliers. This makes sense since most counties are similar with a low pop density, with a few high density populated outliers like Cook County, Illinois, causing the boxplot to look like a flat line. Since it's extremely right-skewed, as seen in the histogram from Q1, the boxplot is pushed to the bottom.

## Q3: Scatterplot below poverty vs. college-educated

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = state, shape = state)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  labs(
    x = "People with a College Degree (%)", 
    y = "People Below Poverty (%)", 
    title = "People Below Poverty vs. College-Educated")
```

Answer: the scatterplot shows a negative relationship between the percentage of people with a college degree and those living below the poverty line. Higher percentages of college education tend to have lower poverty rates, and vice versa, with several outliers. One clear outlier is Jackson, Illinois, which has a relatively high percentage below poverty (about 28%) despite having a higher percentage of college-educated people (about 37%). The states seem to vary somewhat in their strength and spread, such as Indiana seems to have tighter clustering compared to Minnesota. While this overall relationship appears to be consistent across states, it's difficult to discern due to how cluttered the graph is. I would not be confident commenting on specific trends by state, but this graph does help show the overall relationship across midwest counties.

## Q4: Scatterplot faceted by state

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = state, shape = state)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_wrap(~state) + 
  labs(
    x = "People with a College Degree (%)", 
    y = "People Below Poverty (%)", 
    title = "People Below Poverty vs. College-Educated by State")
```

Answer: I think it depends on the question being asked. I like Q3s plot better for understanding the overall trend of the midwest, but this scatterplot is so much easier to look at the relationship between poverty and college education on an individual state basis, as it's less cluttered. This one also may highlight differences in strength and shape of the relationship that was more difficult when they were overlapped.

## Q5: Do some states have counties that tend to be geographically larger than others?

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = state, y = area)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs(
    x = "State", 
    y = "Area",
    title = "Distribution of County Area by State")
```

Answer: Yes, some states have geographically larger counties on average than others. For example, counties in Minnesota tend to have larger median areas compared to counties in states such as Ohio and Indiana, and also has an outlier with the largest county area, St. Louis County. Illinois, Minnesota, and Wisconsin also have greater variation in county size, as seen by their wider spread. Whereas Indiana and Ohio have much shorter distributions, suggesting their county areas are more consistent in size.

## Q6: Do some states have a higher percentage of their counties located in a metropolitan area?

```{r}
midwest <- midwest |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Yes", "No"))

ggplot(midwest, aes(x = state, fill = metro)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "fill") + 
  labs(x = "State", 
       y = "Proportion of Counties",
       title = "Proportion of Counties in Metropolitan Areas by State")
```

Answer: Yes, some states have a higher percentage of their counties located in metropolitan areas than others. Ohio appears to have the highest proportion of metro counties at about 45%. Indiana also has a relatively high proportion of metro counties at about 40%. In contrast, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin have a lower percentage of counties in metropolitan areas, with metro counties making up about 26%, 27%, and 26% of all counties respectively.

#Q7: Recreating scatterplot

```{r}
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = percwhite)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_wrap(~state) + 
  scale_color_gradient(low='black', high='blue') + 
  labs(
    x='% college educated', 
    y='% below poverty line',
    title='Percentage of White People Below Poverty vs. \nCollege-Educated by State',
    color = "% white") + 
  theme_minimal()
```

Answer: Menominee County, Wisconsin, is a clear outlier. This county no black people (0%), very few "Other" (less than 1%), and a relatively (to other counties) low percentage of white people (about 11%), while the majority of the population (about 88%) is classified as “amerindian," which I'm assuming refers to Indigenous peoples.

# Part 2: North Carolina

```{r, echo = false}
nc_county <- read_csv("data/nc-county.csv")
```

## Q8: pop density vs area

Answer 1: Given what we've seen in previous states (although this is a completely diff region), I might guess that there's a negative relationship, especially since I can't think of any major metropolitan areas that would have high pop densities.

```{r}
ggplot(nc_county, aes(x = land_area_mi2, y = density)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  labs(x = "Land Area (square miles)", 
       y = "Population Density\n(people per square mile)",
       title = "Population Density vs. Land Area in\nNorth Carolina Counties",
       subtitle = "According to 2020 census data")
```

Answer 2: there is sort of a positive relationship between land area and population density, but the trend is relatively flat, where population density is relatively low overall. There are several outliers, likely metropolitan areas w/ very high population density despite smaller land area. I was not correct.

## Q9: pop density vs land area in square meters

```{r}
ggplot(nc_county, aes(x = land_area_m2, y = density)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  labs(
    x = "Land Area\n(square meters)", 
    y = "Population Density\n(people per square mile)",
    title = "Population Density vs. Land Area in\nNorth Carolina Counties",
    subtitle = "According to 2020 census data")
```

Answer: this plot shows an identical negative relationship as the previous plot. The only difference is the scale of the x-axis, where values are much larger in square meters and slightly stretches the points horizontally, but the overall relationship is unchanged.
